prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: West, Past, When

outputs.L1:
For twenty years I have lived within half a mile of it. Facing west, guided by the black iron weather-hen half-strangled in clematis atop the garage roof, I can trace its location: past a low ridge in the limestone cliff face of the dale lies a cave concealed among the bushes. Long after the old tigers had vanished, leaving only their teeth behind, the valley people would climb to this place bearing those among their dead they deemed most worthy—pressing them deep within, drawing them out again, parading them about: "They're coming! They're coming!"

We Malagasy cherish our second burials. We engage a band that arrives by van. Once more, with the flesh nearly dissolved, we gather our beloved dead into our arms. They fall from their grave-clothes in soft fragments, much as food falls from a can for a dog. We wrap them anew in fresh, dry linen. Their presence blesses our lives with contentment. We carry them in procession through the valley—here setting down a finger as offering to the god who takes the form of rat or raven, there a small bone to be placed beneath the hearth for good fortune.

And what, then, was fortune? In those days, the afterlife held a modest span: nothing so excessive as eternity, nothing so rigid as duty. The afterlife, rather, would arrive to join the celebration.
outputs.L2:
For two decades now, I've resided within a stone's throw—half a mile, to be precise—of this spot. I can pinpoint it by heading west from the garage roof, where a black iron weathervane shaped like a rooster sits nearly choked by clematis vines. Beyond a small rise in the limestone dale's rock face lies a cave tucked among the bushes.

Long after the ancient tigers vanished, leaving only their teeth behind, the people of the valley would make the climb up there bearing their most treasured dead. They'd push the bodies deep inside, then retrieve them, parade them about, chanting "They're coming! They're coming!" We Malagasies hold a deep affection for the ritual of second burial. A band arrives by van, hired for the occasion.

Once decomposition has nearly run its course, we cradle our beloved dead once more in our embrace. Fragments slip from the burial shrouds—falling much like dog food tumbles from its tin. We swaddle them anew in crisp, dry linen. Their presence brings joy and blessing to our lives. We carry them in procession around the valley, leaving offerings along the way: a finger here for the deity who takes the form of rat or raven, a foot bone there, tucked beneath the hearth to bring good fortune.

But what did fortune mean, exactly? In those days, the afterlife had reasonable boundaries—nothing as extreme as endless eternity, nothing rigid or regimented. The afterlife, back then, was willing to join in the festivities.
outputs.L3:
# The Cave in the Limestone Dale

For twenty years now, I have lived within sight of the limestone dale, and in all that time I have never lost my way to the cave hidden within its folds. I find it the same way each time: first spotting the weathervane that catches the light from the farmhouse below, then following the familiar ridge of cliff that rises like a spine along the valley's edge. These landmarks have become so ingrained in me that I could probably walk the path blind, guided only by memory and the particular slope of the land beneath my feet.

The cave itself carries a weight of history far older than my two decades of acquaintance with it. Long before I ever set foot in this valley, the ancient people who lived here practiced a custom both strange and tender: they would carry their dead into the cave's depths, only to bring them out again, and then return them once more, in a cycle that seemed to defy the finality we now associate with death. Each time the dead emerged, the living would cry out with genuine joy—"They're coming!"—as though welcoming home travelers from a long journey rather than confronting the stillness of mortality.

This practice echoes, in striking ways, the Malagasy tradition of *famadihana*, or second burials, which persists in Madagascar to this day. In this ritual, families hire musicians—a full band—to provide the celebratory atmosphere befitting such an occasion. They wait until decomposition has progressed to its later stages, when the body has largely liquefied, and then they perform the remarkable act of physically embracing and holding their deceased loved one once again. It is a reunion in the most literal sense, a chance to touch and hold what was once thought lost forever.

The ritual does not end with this embrace. The dead are carefully rewrapped in fresh linen, their old shrouds replaced with new cloth as if preparing them for another stage of existence. Then begins a procession—the body paraded joyfully around the valley, accompanied by music and celebration rather than mourning. During this journey, portions of the body are distributed as offerings to various forces believed to govern fortune and fate: a finger might be given to appease a rat god, or perhaps a raven deity, while a small fragment of bone finds its way beneath the hearth of a home, meant to secure luck and prosperity for the family who dwells there.

What strikes me most about these traditions—both the ancient valley practice and its Malagasy counterpart—is how radically different their conception of the afterlife was from what we might expect. Death, in this framework, was not eternal, nor was it treated with the somber solemnity we so often associate with mortality. Instead, the afterlife was imagined as something finite, something communal, something that existed in relationship with the living rather than in permanent separation from them. It was, in the words that best capture this sensibility, something that "would come to the party"—an active participant in the ongoing life of the community, rather than a distant and unreachable state of being.
outputs.L4:
# The Turning of the Bones

There was a cave near my grandmother's house, not far from where the road narrowed into red dirt and the rice paddies began their terraced descent toward the river. As children we were told not to go there, which of course meant we went, pressing our small bodies against the cool limestone walls, feeling for the places where the rock had been worn smooth by generations of hands. We didn't understand yet what those hands had been doing. We only knew the cave held something the adults spoke of in lowered voices, something that belonged to the dead but was not exactly *about* death—not in the way the missionaries' stories were about death, with their gates and their scales and their eternal sortings.

I think of that cave now when I think of famadihana, though the turning of the bones happens in tombs, not caves—stone houses built above ground, painted sometimes, tended like second homes. But the cave taught me the same lesson the tombs would later teach: that the dead do not simply depart. They wait. They remain in relationship, folded into the geography of a place, and periodically they ask—or rather, we ask on their behalf, through the fabric and the music and the aged rum poured into the earth—to be remembered in the flesh of ritual rather than only in the abstraction of grief.

To exhume a body is not a metaphor. The word famadihana means, literally, the turning over. Every few years, sometimes five, sometimes seven, the family gathers at the tomb—and it is a serious gathering, requiring money saved, silk purchased, animals slaughtered for the feast that will follow. The stone door of the tomb is opened. Someone must go inside. The air is different in there, thick with the particular staleness of enclosed stone, and the smell that is not quite rot anymore, because enough time has passed, because the body has done what bodies do and has become something else: bone wrapped in what remains of the burial cloth, sometimes dust, sometimes still recognizably a shape that was once a shape you knew.

The remains are brought out into the light. This is the part the tourist accounts skip over, or render sentimental, but there is nothing especially soft about it. Hands do the work. Old cloth, disintegrating, is peeled back, and new silk—lamba mena, the red shroud, though it is not always red, sometimes white, sometimes patterned—is wound around what is left. This is done by family members, not specialists, not undertakers. Your aunt does this. Your father's cousin does this. The great-grandmother whose face you have only known from a photograph is rewrapped by the granddaughter who has her nose.

There is music. There is dancing—the corpse is sometimes lifted and carried, almost danced with, around the tomb, shoulder-borne, while the living move to the sound of the brass band hired for the occasion. This detail unsettles people who hear about it secondhand, the idea of dancing with the dead, but it unsettles less once you understand what death is being asked to mean here. Not an ending to be honored from a respectful distance. A relationship to be maintained, actively, with the same physical intimacy that characterized the relationship in life—the touching, the adjusting of cloth, the carrying.

What strikes me, returning to this practice through the memory of that childhood cave, is how small the metaphysics are, how unconcerned with eternity. The ancestors are not imagined as residing in some far celestial architecture, judged and placed. They are here, in the tomb on the hillside, in the cave in the limestone, subject to weather and time and the attention of their descendants. Their continued existence is not guaranteed by an already-settled cosmic order; it is sustained by the labor of memory, cloth, and gathering. If the family forgets, if the fady—the taboos, the obligations—go unmet, something is lost, but it's a social loss, a relational one, not a cosmic catastrophe. The afterlife here is modest. It asks only to be periodically renewed.

This modesty is, I've come to think, its own kind of mercy. A death that must be maintained rather than merely mourned is a death that keeps you occupied, keeps your hands busy with cloth and your body busy with dance, keeps the terrible finality at bay by giving you tasks. Grief in the famadihana tradition is not something you sit with alone, staring at an unbridgeable gap between the living and the dead. It is something you do, with your family, every few years, in the particular light of the Highland afternoon, with rum passed hand to hand and the band playing something almost cheerful.

I do not know what the people who avoided that cave near my grandmother's house believed about what was inside it—whether it held ancestors properly attended to, or ancestors forgotten, their tombs untended, their names slipping out of the mouths of the living. I know only that the cave held its silence the way all such places do, patiently, waiting to see if anyone would come back for the bones.
outputs.L5:
# When the West Looks Back

There is a peculiar melancholy that settles over Western civilization when it turns to examine its own past. Unlike cultures that view history as an unbroken thread connecting ancestors to descendants, the West often treats its history as a foreign country—fascinating, sometimes admirable, but fundamentally *other*.

This creates a strange paradox. When we study ancient Rome, we marvel at its engineering, its law, its literature—yet we distance ourselves from its brutality, its slavery, its conquests. When we examine the Enlightenment, we celebrate its championing of reason and human rights, while simultaneously reckoning with the colonialism it helped justify. The West seems perpetually caught between reverence and repudiation for what came before.

This tension isn't merely academic. It shapes contemporary identity in profound ways. When politicians invoke "Western values," they're selectively curating a past—choosing which threads to celebrate and which to disown. The Renaissance becomes a story of human achievement, rarely mentioned alongside the Inquisition happening simultaneously. The founding of democratic institutions gets separated from the exclusions that defined them for centuries.

Perhaps this is simply how any civilization must process its history—through selective memory, through narrative construction, through the uncomfortable work of holding contradiction. The West is not unique in mythologizing its past, only perhaps more self-conscious about doing so, more prone to public debate about which version of history should prevail.

When we ask "when did the West begin?"—with Athens? Jerusalem? Rome? The Enlightenment?—we're really asking a different question: what do we want to become, and which ancestors do we choose to claim as our own?

The past doesn't change, but our relationship to it does. And in that relationship lies the ongoing project of understanding not just where the West has been, but where it might yet go.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about the Malagasy famadihana (turning of the bones) tradition, blending personal narrative with cultural ritual detail.
counterfactuals.output:
**Turning**

They tell me the dead grow cold in their silk, that every seven years the ancestors ask to be warmed again by the sun and by our hands, and so we come, my father's whole family, up the red clay path to the hillside where the tomb sits like a stone house facing east, and we bring rum for the ones who can no longer drink it, and rice pressed into small white mountains, and a brass band that will not stop playing until the bones are laughing too.

I was eleven the first time I held my great-grandmother. Not her face — that had gone back to the earth years before, the way faces do — but the long brown architecture of her, femur and rib and the small stones of her hands, wrapped in the old lamba gone the color of weak tea, unraveling at the edges like a secret finally let out. My grandfather said, *she is not resting, she is only waiting*, and he lifted her the way you'd lift a sleeping child too heavy for your arms but yours anyway, and I understood then that the tomb is not a place we put people to forget them but a room we visit to remember harder.

We danced with her. This is the part no one believes when I tell it outside Madagascar — that we hoisted the bound bodies to our shoulders and moved with them through the crowd, feet finding the rhythm the way water finds a slope, aunts weeping and laughing in the same breath, someone's cousin drunk on toaka gasy shouting the family news into the dry bones' ear as if they'd only been away at market: *your granddaughter is married now, the harvest was good, we still fight over the same stretch of land.* The dead were given new silk, red and white, wound tight and clean, and for an hour they were not memory but weight, not story but shoulder-ache, not ancestor but aunt, grandfather, sister, held up into the sun one more time before the stone door closed again.

I think of this now in another country, in a room with no hillside, no tomb, no lamba folded in a cedar chest waiting its seven years. My dead here are ash in a box on a shelf, and I do not know how to dance with ash. But I remember the weight of her on my shoulder, how the bones did not feel like absence but like argument — *I am still here, I am still yours, do not let the walking ones forget how to carry me.*

So this is what I do instead: I say her name into rooms she never entered. I pour something bright into a glass and do not drink it, not yet. I imagine the tomb on the red hill still standing, the doors closed on cool dark bones warming themselves on memory until the family comes again, until someone young enough to still believe in ceremony lifts what is left of her into the light, unafraid, and calls it love because it is.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of literary fiction that starts with precise geographic directions to a hidden cave and gradually reveals a family's ancestral burial customs.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Dry Place

*Begin at the fork where the county road forgets its name and becomes gravel. Go two hundred paces north, keeping the fence line on your left hand until it ends at a fallen chestnut. Cross the creek at its narrowest point, where three flat stones break the water like the knuckles of a fist. Climb the ridge bearing slightly east, past the split hickory struck by lightning the year of the flood. The cave mouth is hidden by a curtain of catbrier; you must part it like a door.*

I have these directions memorized, though I carry the paper anyway, soft as cloth now from being folded and unfolded across three generations. My grandmother wrote them in pencil on the back of a seed catalog page, and my mother copied them onto good stationery when the pencil began to fade, and I have copied them again into the back of my father's ledger, in the space where he used to record the weight of his cattle. The directions have outlived the fence, which fell in a windstorm decades ago and was never rebuilt, its cedar posts gone soft and swallowed by blackberry. They have outlived the chestnut, too—all the chestnuts, taken by blight before I was born—so that "the fallen chestnut" is now simply a shape in my mind, a place where the ground dips a certain way, and I have learned to trust the dip.

I am carrying my father in a flour sack.

Not all of him. Just what is left after two years in the ground behind the house, which is our custom, though I did not understand it as a custom until I was grown and mentioned it to my husband's family and watched their faces do something complicated and careful, the way faces do when they are deciding not to be frightened in front of you.

This is how it goes. When someone dies, we bury them in the kitchen garden, in the plot my great-great-grandfather cleared for this exact purpose, which is why nothing grows there but chives, which come back every spring whether we want them or not, pushing up through whoever is currently resting below. We mark the place with a flat stone, unlettered. We wait two years—not one, not three, but two, though no one living remembers why, only that my grandmother was firm on the number, said it the way you'd say a law of physics. Two years is how long it takes, she said, for a person to finish being a body and start being bone.

Then we dig them up.

I did this for my father in October, on a day the color of a knife blade, with my son standing beside me holding the lantern though we didn't need it yet, the sun still up, because he wanted a task and I understood that. The chives had gone gold and were folding down into the earth for winter. I dug with the shovel that has done this work for four generations, its handle replaced twice, its blade never. When I reached the flat stone I set it aside and kept going, more carefully now, using the trowel, then my hands, until I found what was left of him.

It is not so terrible as you might imagine. Two years is enough time. The clay in our valley is heavy and does its work slowly but thoroughly, and by the time we open the ground again there is only the good clean architecture of a person—no smell, no horror, just the pale geometry of what held him up all those years he was walking around being loud and particular and mine. I washed the bones in the creek, the same creek the directions cross, kneeling in the cold water with my son handing me each piece as I asked for it, femur, rib, the small mysterious bones of the hand, and I want to tell you it was terrible and it was not terrible, it was the most ordinary thing I have ever done, like washing dishes after a meal that took a lifetime to cook.

We wrapped him in the linen my mother wove for this purpose before she died—she wove one for herself, too, without telling me, and I found it in the cedar chest after her funeral, folded with a note that said *for later, whenever later is*, and later has already happened, she is already up in the cave with everyone else, and I did not think to mention this before because grief has its own directions and I am still learning to follow them.

So: the fork, the fence line, the chestnut that isn't there anymore, the creek, the hickory split by lightning, the catbrier curtain. My son goes ahead of me now, twelve years old and solemn with the importance of his task, parting the vines with both hands the way you'd part a beaded doorway in an old house.

The cave is not large. You would not find it impressive if you did not know what it held. A single chamber, dry as the directions promise, floored with fine dust that never seems to increase no matter how many years pass. And along the walls, on shelves my ancestors cut into the limestone by hand, generation after generation of us, arranged not in coffins or boxes but simply laid out, femur beside femur, skull nested in the crook of an arm that held it eighty years before either of them expected to be here together like this.

There is no order to it that a stranger could read. But I can read it. There is my grandmother, third shelf, second from the left, and beside her the space that was empty for eleven years until my mother joined her, the two of them together again the way they were before either of them was a widow. There is my great-uncle who died at nineteen in a war nobody talks about anymore, his bones smaller than you'd expect, and beside him the space my grandmother saved for sixty years, refusing to let anyone else be laid there, because she said a mother keeps a place at the table even after the table has been put away.

I find the space I have already chosen for my father—beside his own mother, who died when he was eleven, whom he barely remembered but spoke of often, inventing memories he wanted to have had. I lay him down. My son helps me, and does not flinch, because this is the fourth time he has done this and he no longer thinks of it as strange, he thinks of it as simply what happens, the way rain happens, the way seasons happen.

We do not pray, exactly. My mother used to say something in the old language, a handful of words that came down to her the way the directions did, worn soft with use, and I say them now though I don't know precisely what they mean anymore, only that they are the words you say, the way you'd say *goodnight* without thinking about what night or good actually mean.

Afterward we sit for a while in the cave's cool quiet, my son leaning against me, and I think about the two years of waiting that are already beginning again somewhere else—my aunt, this time, gone in the spring, resting now beneath the chives at the house, patient as clay, becoming what she will become. I think about the directions I will write someday, in pencil probably, because that is how it started and I like the thought of it wearing thin again, being copied again, outliving whatever new thing falls where the chestnut used to be.

I think about my own bones, which will lie somewhere on this wall eventually, and whose hands will wash them, and whether they will understand, the way I did not understand for so long, that this is not about death at all. It is about the two-year distance between a body and a name. It is about learning to let a person finish becoming what they will always be to you, which is not flesh, which was never really flesh, but architecture—the frame that held up everything you loved, laid finally to rest beside all the other frames, in the dry dark, keeping each other's shape.

We leave before dark. My son parts the catbrier for me on the way out, the same gesture, reversed, and I fold the directions and put them back in my pocket, though I no longer need to look at them.

I could walk this path with my eyes closed. I expect, eventually, someone will have to.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an evocative, poetic short story exploring second burial rites in Madagascar, using unsettling imagery and dark humor.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Turning

Grandmother's bones had grown restless, Dada said, which was why we dug her up on a Tuesday smelling of rain and woodsmoke.

"She wants to dance," my aunt Voahangi announced, hands on hips, surveying the tomb like a woman inspecting a disappointing cake. "Seven years in the ground and no one's aired her out. Rude, that's what it is."

The tomb breathed a smell like old library books left in a swamp. Cousin Fara gagged, then laughed, then gagged again—that particular rhythm of the recently horrified. We unwrapped Grandmother's lamba, and there she was: not the woman who'd braided my hair too tight, but something smaller, umber, architectural. A xylophone wearing her Sunday scarf.

"She's lost weight," Uncle Rakoto said. "Death agrees with her figure."

The band arrived at dusk—two men with a valiha and a drum that had clearly seen its own share of famadihanas, its skin stretched thin as gossip. Music unspooled into the humid air, and we lifted Grandmother onto our shoulders, this bundle of her, light as a secret, and we danced.

This is the part no one tells you: how funny grief becomes when you're spinning a corpse-wrapped grandmother above a crowd of shrieking children, how the old women cackle wickedly, calling out her flirtations from decades past—*Bao! Remember when you kissed the schoolteacher behind the rice paddy?*—as though the dead might blush, as though bones could still hold shame.

We spoke to her. We always speak to them.

"Your grandson failed his exams," Voahangi confided into the wrapped skull, conversational as gossip over fence-posts. "Perhaps you could intervene. Death has surely improved your influence with these matters."

The children touched her feet for luck and shrieked with delighted horror, the particular thrill of touching what should not be touched. Somewhere a baby cried; somewhere else, someone opened a bottle of rum with their teeth. The dead, I've come to think, love a party more than the living do—they have so little else to attend.

By moonrise, we rewrapped her in fresh silk, softer than her old shroud, softer than skin, though skin was a rumor by now, a story her bones told about themselves. We placed her with her kinsmen, all those other quiet architectures, all that stacked geometry of family. The tomb sealed her in like a secret finally told correctly.

"Until next time, Neny," Dada whispered, patting the stone as one pats a horse, or a debt, or a door you're not sure will open again.

Walking home, I thought about how we handle our dead the way we handle our shame: hauling it out periodically, dancing with it, dressing it in something nicer, then putting it back to ferment in the dark—not because we've forgiven or forgotten, but because forgetting was never the point.

The point was the touching. The point was: *you still count. You are still ours. Even folded down to essential architecture, even reduced to your most honest shape—we will still come to find you, still lift you toward the light, still whisper our failures into the hollow o of your ear, hoping you might, from wherever the dead file their complaints, put in a good word.*

Grandmother's bones, I think, were satisfied. They'd had their dance. They'd heard their gossip. 

They could rest now, until the next Tuesday smelling of rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical narrative voice piece where a speaker describes exhuming and re-wrapping the bones of loved ones during a traditional ceremony, incorporating sensory and emotional detail.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Second Burial

I have come with clean cloth and clean hands
to the hill where you have waited three years for me,
learning the language of roots, the slow patience of soil.

They say the earth keeps what we cannot,
holds the body the way grief holds a name—
tight, then looser, then a shape we can carry.

When they lift the stone, the smell rises first:
not rot, not anymore, but something older,
mineral, like rain on hot ground, like the inside of a cave.
I do not flinch. I have been told not to flinch.
This is not the ending. This is the folding-in.

Your bones are lighter than I remember your hands being,
lighter than the weight of you leaning on my shoulder
that last winter, when you still had opinions about soup,
about which grandchild forgot to call.

They pass you to me piece by piece,
the small architecture of what held you upright—
femur, rib, the delicate wing-bones of your feet
that walked you to market every morning for sixty years.

I wash you with water and wine,
my thumb finding the smooth worn places
where you were once a man, once a girl,
once someone's whole reason for coming home.

The women beside me hum something
older than the hill itself,
a song with no edges, only circles,
and I find my mouth knows the shape of it too,
though I have never been taught.

I wrap you now in white,
new cloth against old bone,
the way you wrapped me once, I'm told,
when I was new and did not yet know
what it meant to be held.

This is not goodbye.
I said that three years ago, weeping,
thinking the earth would keep you forever,
not knowing forever has its own seasons,
its own need to be opened, aired, re-blessed.

We are all just waiting to be gathered again—
by daughters, by earth, by the small persistent hands
of those who loved us enough
to come back for what remains,
to hold what is light enough now to carry,
to say: *I remember you whole,
and I will make you whole again,
even in pieces,
even in bone,
even in this last, tender architecture
of love.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a surreal, densely imagistic passage about death rituals, ancestor worship, and the afterlife, mixing anthropological references with intimate first-person reflection.
counterfactuals.output:
They say the dead must be fed before they can be believed. In the highlands—any highlands, all highlands, the ones that exist only in the footnotes of dissertations no one finishes—the mourners bring rice wrapped in banana leaf and set it at the threshold like a bribe to a customs officer. *Liminal*, the anthropologists write, meaning *neither*, meaning *both*, meaning the corpse is a door that has forgotten which way it swings.

My grandmother kept her mother's molars in a jam jar on the windowsill, next to the sun-tea and the desiccated aloe. She called this an altar. I called it Tuesday. The teeth yellowed further in the light, as if still chewing on something the living couldn't taste—cardamom, maybe, or the specific grief of outliving your own hunger.

*Field notes, undated:* The Toraja keep their dead as boarders. Grandfather sits at the table in his good suit for years, fed tobacco, informed of the harvest, his skin darkening to teak, his silence mistaken—correctly—for patience. This is called *to makula'*, the sick one, a euphemism so total it becomes a kind of love. I have done this with photographs. I have poured coffee for a man who has been ash since March, watched the steam rise and bend toward the empty chair like something magnetized, like grief has its own gravity and the coffee simply obeys.

There is a village—I will not say where, because it may only exist between two paragraphs in a book I read at seventeen and half-remember now as scripture—where they paint the bones of the dead with red ochre and dance them through the streets once a decade. *Famadihana.* The turning of the bones. Sisters unwrap their mothers like presents. The mother is dry and light as a wasp's nest. She is passed hand to hand above the crowd, and someone's baby is held up to touch her ribcage for luck, for continuity, for the simple electric fact of two bodies in the same lineage occupying the same air.

I touched my father's hand in the hospital and it had already gone somewhere without him. Anthropology has a word for this too, some Latinate scaffolding to hold up the fact that a hand can be a hand and also a departure gate. I don't remember the word. I remember the temperature.

The Egyptians packed the body with linen and natron and small blue faience animals meant to answer for you in the afterlife should your name be called and your mouth be otherwise occupied with dissolving. *Ushabti*, the answerer. I have thought since then that we are all walking around with small blue substitutes buried in our chests, waiting to speak for us when we cannot speak for ourselves—at the deathbed, at the eulogy, in the long insomniac hour when the ceiling asks are you still here and something smaller than you, older than you, made of dream-clay and inherited fear, answers *present, present, still here.*

At the funeral, the paid mourners wailed in a language I didn't recognize as language until I recognized it as mine—the same sound my grandmother made stirring the pot too fast, a small keening under the domestic, ancestral, encoded like a watermark. Grief, it turns out, is also field data. It repeats across cultures with such fidelity that I begin to suspect the dead are not so much gone as *encrypted*, waiting for the right ritual key: salt on the doorstep, a coin under the tongue, forty-nine days of chanting, a jar of teeth on a windowsill catching afternoon light like something almost, almost about to bite down on the world again.

I set a plate for my father on his birthday. I don't believe in it. I do it anyway, the way you keep speaking a dead language because your mouth has not yet been informed of the extinction. Somewhere—the anthropologists are certain of this, and so, on my knees at 2 a.m. with an untouched plate of his favorite dumplings cooling on the table, am I—somewhere the dead are also setting a place. For us. Practicing the shapes of our names with mouths made of ash and ochre and old teeth, waiting for the day we arrive hungry, and known, and finally fluent in whatever it is they've been trying to say all along.
